title: Proving all cases and unique solutions
transcript: A proof needs reasons that cover every allowed case. To prove a unique answer, show that it works and that every different answer fails. A bound or an increasing pattern can eliminate an entire range in one step.

AMC practice may ask for the only integer satisfying a clue. Use the constraint to get a narrow range before testing candidates. Mawa application practice rewards clear reasons. A proof can use inequalities, a complete list, or a pattern you justify for all values.
List the multiples of five from twenty through thirty-two, counting both endpoints. Explain how you know the list is complete. Find the first eligible multiple and step forward by the divisor.

The first eligible value is twenty. The preceding multiple is fifteen, below the lower limit. The full list is twenty, twenty-five and thirty. The next multiple is thirty-five, which is already above the upper limit.
Two positive whole numbers add to seventeen. Neither can exceed twelve. List all pairs, counting a swapped pair only once. Call the smaller number x and use this to bound x from both sides.

The larger number is seventeen minus x, so x is at least five. Since x is the smaller, it is at most eight. Each integer in that range gives exactly one partner. There are four pairs. All of them meet the cap.

An integer-sided rectangle has area one hundred and thirty-five square units. Its longer side is six units greater than its shorter side. Find its two side lengths and prove that no second pair of positive integer lengths works.

Let x be the shorter side. The area is x times x plus six, with both terms positive. Try eight for x and check the area. The next integer, nine, gives nine times fifteen, exactly one hundred and thirty-five. That proves this pair exists.

Every increase in x increases both positive factors. The area increases strictly. Any x below nine gives too little area and any x above gives too much. The dimensions are therefore uniquely nine and fifteen units. They check both the area and the side difference.

One candidate that works proves existence only. Give a bound, exhaustive list or increasing rule to exclude every other candidate. When working with a closed interval, its boundary values are eligible. Test whether the inequality is strict before dropping an endpoint.

State what you need to prove: all answers, at least one answer, or exactly one answer. List the restrictions that define a legal candidate. Use a complete range or a justified relationship. Verify the survivor or survivors in the original problem before writing your answer.
